hooks.text: Voyager 2 launched two weeks before its twin, yet was named second.
The only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune launched before its twin.
Only one spacecraft has ever visited Uranus and Neptune.

title: The Twin That Launched First
description: Discover why Voyager 2 launched before its twin and became the only probe to visit Uranus and Neptune.

beats.text: Voyager 2 launched two weeks before its twin, yet was named second.
beats.visual: Titan IIIE rocket launching Voyager 2 from Cape Canaveral, 1977

beats.text: Most people naturally assume the lower numbered spacecraft went up first.
beats.visual: NASA artist's concept of the Voyager spacecraft in space, 1977

beats.text: In 1977, NASA relied on a rare planetary alignment occurring once every 176 years.
beats.visual: Planetary alignment diagram for the Grand Tour mission, 1977

beats.text: Voyager 1 took a shorter and faster trajectory, reaching Jupiter and Saturn sooner.
beats.visual: Full disk image of Jupiter taken by Voyager 1, 1979

beats.text: Meanwhile, the truly first-launched probe simply took a much slower path.
beats.visual: NASA artist's concept of Voyager 2 trajectory, 1977

beats.text: That brilliant cosmic detour made Voyager 2 the only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune.
beats.visual: Full disk image of Uranus taken by Voyager 2, 1986

beats.text: It discovered hidden rings and dozens of new moons before diving completely south into interstellar space.
beats.visual: Full disk image of Neptune showing the Great Dark Spot, 1989

beats.text: That is precisely why Voyager 2 launched two weeks before its twin, yet was named second.
beats.visual: Deep Space Station 43 antenna in Australia, 2020

better_than_last: This episode applies the myth_vs_fact structure by opening with a counter-intuitive chronological fact, hitting the required word count of 115 words total, and resolving it smoothly with the unique planetary destination achievement.
